title: Knowledge Check 9: Lessons 65-72
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 65-72 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: In an enterprise AI reference architecture, what distinct job does each of the three core patterns perform?
options: RAG grounds answers in governed enterprise data, the agent platform hosts and orchestrates agents, and the LLM gateway controls model access, cost, and failover.
RAG controls model access and cost, the agent platform grounds answers in enterprise data, and the LLM gateway hosts and orchestrates a fleet of agents across teams.
RAG hosts and orchestrates agents, the agent platform routes every model call to a provider, and the LLM gateway grounds answers by retrieving passages from the index.
All three patterns perform essentially the same job of grounding, routing, and orchestrating, and differ only in the vendor that supplies each component.
questions.explanation: The three patterns compose but never overlap: RAG is the grounding subsystem for facts, the agent platform is the runtime for reasoning, memory, and tools, and the LLM gateway is the control plane for model access, cost, and failover.

questions.question: Why does model traffic need a gateway built for LLM calls rather than a general-purpose API gateway?
options: Request-count limits track capacity precisely because every model call consumes the same number of units regardless of its size and shape.
A general-purpose gateway cannot authenticate the callers that reach a model provider, so it must always be replaced before any model traffic is allowed.
Model cost and capacity are measured in tokens, so a request-count limit cannot track spend or fail over across providers.
Model providers refuse any traffic that has passed through a general-purpose gateway, so a purpose-built gateway is the only option.
questions.explanation: LLM cost and capacity scale with tokens, not request counts, so a request-count limit lets one user spend a token budget of any size and cannot apply semantic caching or multi-provider failover.

questions.question: When every application team integrates with model providers on its own, what capability does the enterprise lose, and what restores it?
options: It loses nothing at all, because each team calling providers directly is simpler, cheaper, and faster to operate than any shared infrastructure ever could be.
It loses the single governed point where budget, access logging, and model swaps are enforced, and a gateway restores one centralized control point.
It loses the ability to ground answers in enterprise data, which a gateway restores by retrieving and augmenting prompts before generation.
It loses the ability to store embeddings, which a gateway restores by maintaining the vector index for every consuming application.
questions.explanation: Direct provider integration leaves no one place to enforce budget, log access, or swap models, so a provider pivot becomes a rewrite of every caller; the gateway turns model selection into one governed, centralized decision.

questions.question: What value does continuous integration add to a Salesforce team's delivery lifecycle?
options: It replaces the need for a branching strategy entirely by merging all work directly into production on a fixed schedule every night.
It merges every change into a shared main line often and validates each merge, so integration problems surface early and cheaply.
It removes the need for source control because every change is automatically tested before it can reach the production org.
It ships every change straight to production on each merge without any separate validation or review step.
questions.explanation: Continuous integration validates every merge to the shared main line, so a change that breaks the build is caught the day it is merged rather than the week before release, when the fix is far more expensive.

questions.question: An org deploys a release successfully. What does it take to know the change is actually working in production?
options: Waiting for the next release, because only the following version can reveal whether the prior one actually held up in front of real users.
Completing the deployment, because a successful deploy proves the change behaves correctly in production.
Observing the release through logs, metrics, and traces, because a deployment is not the same as a working system.
Validating the change set in a sandbox, because pre-production testing is the final and definitive check.
questions.explanation: A deployment moves metadata, a release makes it visible, and a working system is known only by watching evidence in production; observability is what closes the loop that a successful deployment leaves open.

questions.question: Why is a branching strategy best treated as a governance decision rather than a tooling detail?
options: The branching strategy is a governance decision that sets who may merge, how often, and what must be true first.
The branching strategy is a tooling detail that only affects where files are physically stored and how quickly they can be checked out.
The branching strategy matters only for teams that have never adopted continuous integration or automated testing.
The branching strategy can safely be deferred until the team is already under pressure to ship a release.
questions.explanation: The branching strategy decides who can merge, how often, and what has to be true before a merge is allowed; without that decision, teams accumulate merge conflicts that surface at the worst possible moment, release time.

questions.question: What two separate problems do single sign-on and user provisioning each solve?
options: SSO creates the user record in every connected system and provisioning authenticates the person against the identity provider at each login.
SSO handles whether a person can authenticate, while provisioning handles whether a user record exists and stays in sync.
SSO and provisioning are two names for the same identity mechanism working on the very same data in the same system.
Provisioning handles authentication, while SSO manages a user's attributes, groups, and entitlements across applications.
questions.explanation: SSO answers whether a person can get in, and provisioning answers whether a record for that person exists; conflating them designs a system that authenticates people with no record or creates records for people who should not be there.

questions.question: An employee population needs each Salesforce user record to exist before day one and to deactivate when someone leaves. Which approach fits?
options: Just-in-time provisioning, because it creates the record automatically the first time the user logs in and needs no integration to build.
Federation alone, because it authenticates users without ever creating or maintaining a Salesforce user record of any kind.
SCIM provisioning, because it creates, updates, and deactivates records so the user list mirrors the identity provider.
Manual creation in Salesforce, because an administrator should personally approve and type each record by hand.
questions.explanation: SCIM is the right tool when the record must exist ahead of time and stay continuously in sync; it creates, updates, and deactivates user objects so the Salesforce user list faithfully mirrors the identity provider.

questions.question: Employees of a partner firm reach a portal through their own identity provider. When a partner employee leaves, how does access end without the portal owner acting?
options: The partner's identity provider stops issuing the assertions the portal trusts, so the person can no longer authenticate.
The portal's administrator receives an automatic notification and deactivates the account by hand within one business day.
The user record expires automatically after a fixed number of days of inactivity with no action from anyone.
The portal's own directory removes the user as soon as the partner firm reports the departure through a support ticket.
questions.explanation: Federation lets each partner's identity provider vouch for its own people; when an employee leaves, that identity provider stops issuing assertions, so access ends without the portal owner doing anything.

questions.question: A business asks for fast recovery from an outage. What must be defined to turn that wish into a testable target?
options: A single org-wide uptime percentage applied uniformly to every capability, signed off once by IT and never revisited.
The name of the backup vendor and the exact terms of its annual support agreement and escalation contacts.
A recovery time objective and a recovery point objective set per business capability and approved by stakeholders.
A confirmation that platform-level redundancy removes any need for a customer-side recovery target.
questions.explanation: Recovery targets must be measurable and set per capability, because a revenue-critical flow and historical reporting do not warrant the same time to recover or the same tolerance for data loss.

questions.question: A client wants near-zero data loss on financial records but currently only takes daily backups. What is required beyond the daily backup?
options: Nothing more at all, because a daily backup already achieves near-zero data loss for financial records on its own without any extra tooling.
A replication mechanism such as asynchronous event streaming or change data capture, because daily backups cap data loss at a day.
A longer backup retention period, because keeping many older copies on hand reduces the amount of data lost in an outage.
A written service level agreement with the vendor that contractually waives any data loss during an outage.
questions.explanation: A daily backup can never produce a sub-day recovery point, so a near-zero objective on financial records demands a replication mechanism such as event streaming or change data capture, not simply more frequent copies.

questions.question: What does running a restore drill actually establish that an untested backup cannot?
options: That the backup can be restored within the target recovery time and loses no more than the allowed data, proven by a timed test.
That the backup files exist, are complete, and are stored in a separate location from the source data, safely out of reach of the primary org.
That the platform's infrastructure-level failover between data centers is functioning exactly as the vendor designed it.
That the recovery runbook has been written, reviewed, and formally approved by the business stakeholders before any incident.
questions.explanation: A backup is only as real as the restore you have performed; a drill times the actual recovery against the RTO and measures the data lost against the RPO, exposing the gap between the plan and reality while the stakes are a sandbox.

questions.question: When attacking a design scenario, what is the first step, and why does it come before any diagram?
options: Extract the business need and restate the requirements in your own words, so you solve the why rather than the literal wording.
Draw the object model immediately, because the data design drives every other decision that follows, including integration and identity.
Choose the integration technology first, because the chosen pattern determines the entire shape of the solution.
Write the final presentation first, because the board answer should shape the whole design from the very start.
questions.explanation: Solutioning the literal sentences builds whatever the client described instead of what the business needs; restating the why first keeps the whole design pointed at the actual problem.

questions.question: Two systems both claim to own the same piece of data. Why is this the failure that unravels a scenario solution?
options: Because it doubles the storage cost of that data across every system in the client environment, slows every query that reads it, and forces constant reconciliation.
Because when a fact has two owners the copies drift, and any view built on that fact becomes unreliable, so each fact needs one owner.
Because the second owner always performs more slowly than the first one under any realistic production load.
Because it prevents the use of the platform's standard objects for that particular entity in the data model.
questions.explanation: One fact must have one owner; when two systems both claim it, the copies drift apart and take any joined customer view down with them, which is why fixing the system of record comes before integration and data modeling.

questions.question: Which choice reflects how a defensible design handles non-functional requirements?
options: Leave quality expectations general so the client can interpret them once the system is live and in production.
Defer all performance and recovery targets until after the solution has been fully built and tested.
State them as measurable targets chosen to match the client's actual landscape and scale.
Set them to the platform's maximum documented capability regardless of the client's budget, users, or operating reality.
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements with no numbers are not requirements; a defensible design states measurable targets, such as a pricing time or a concurrency level, chosen to fit the client's real peaks, users, and constraints.

questions.question: A team sets its solution SLO equal to the platform SLA. What goes wrong with that choice?
options: A solution SLO should always exceed the platform SLA by a wide margin to be meaningful to users, to demonstrate engineering rigor, and to satisfy auditors.
Platform downtime then consumes the entire error budget, leaving nothing for the application-layer, integration, and maintenance failures the team owns.
The platform SLA is a hard ceiling that a solution SLO can never legally match or exceed in any measurement window.
Equal targets are correct, because the two numbers measure the same thing over the same period and window.
questions.explanation: When the solution SLO equals the platform SLA, any platform outage eats the whole error budget and the team's own failure classes have nothing left to spend, so the solution target is set deliberately below the platform number.

questions.question: What does a well chosen service level indicator measure?
options: The user's actual experience, such as the share of requests that succeed within an acceptable time.
Whether the servers hosting the service are powered on and reachable from the network at any point during the measurement window.
The count of every error a user could cause, including invalid input they typed into a form.
The internal CPU and memory counters of each component in the deployed architecture.
questions.explanation: An SLI measures how well the service is doing from the user's point of view, such as a success rate or a latency threshold, not an internal counter or raw uptime that a person would never feel.

questions.question: When a service has blown its error budget over the trailing window, what does the policy require?
options: Nothing changes at all, because reliability work and feature work are funded from separate and unrelated allowances.
The team permanently freezes all changes, including critical fixes, until the start of the next quarter.
The team halts non-critical changes and focuses on restoring the service until it is back inside its SLO.
The service is retired and rebuilt on a new architecture before any further release is permitted.
questions.explanation: The error budget governs release decisions: while a service is inside its SLO releases proceed, and once it has blown the budget the team halts non-critical changes until reliability work brings it back inside the target.

questions.question: An integration needs every event for a given order observed in sequence, while different orders flow at full throughput. How is this achieved?
options: Route all events for every order to a single partition so that the whole topic keeps one global order of records for all consumers, at the cost of throughput.
Use one separate topic per order so each order has its own independent stream of events that cannot interleave with any other order.
Key each event by the order ID so that order's events land in one partition and stay ordered while other orders proceed in parallel.
Let each consumer sort records after delivery to reconstruct the correct sequence downstream regardless of arrival order.
questions.explanation: Order is guaranteed only within a partition, and records sharing a key land in the same partition; keying by the order ID keeps one order's events ordered while independent orders scatter across partitions and run in parallel.

questions.question: What does a change data capture event record?
options: The row-level state change and when it happened, but not the reason or intent behind it.
The business intent and the specific user action that produced the change, captured at the moment it was made in the source system.
Only deletes and undeletes, never the inserts or updates that the source system makes to its rows.
The full set of prior and current values of the row carried inside every change payload the source emits.
questions.explanation: Change data capture records what happened to the data, complete and non-invasive, but it does not carry the reason, the user, or the intent; a consumer that needs the why must be fed an explicit business event authored at the point of the action.

questions.question: A consumer keeps double-counting the same events after it restarts. What causes this, and what is the fix?
options: Exactly-once delivery failed somewhere in the broker, and the fix is to switch the cluster to a stronger consistency and isolation setting across every partition.
At-least-once delivery re-reads events after a restart, and the fix is to make the consumer idempotent or deduplicate on a stable event ID.
The retention window expired, and the fix is to store a private copy of every event the consumer reads.
The consumer group is unbalanced, and the fix is to add more consumers to rebalance the partitions.
questions.explanation: Streaming platforms default to at-least-once, so a consumer that crashes before committing its offset re-reads events on restart; the design must tolerate that duplicate by making the sink idempotent or deduplicating on an event ID.

questions.question: Why does rejecting an over-budget consumer at the gateway protect the org's shared API request allocation?
options: Because the gateway transparently routes the refused call to a cheaper internal endpoint that does not count against the org allocation at all.
Because a call refused at the gateway never reaches Salesforce, so it consumes the gateway's budget instead of the org's shared allocation.
Because Salesforce raises the allocation cap once the gateway reports that a consumer has been throttled.
Because the gateway's own limits replace the platform's concurrent request limit entirely for every consumer.
questions.explanation: Putting policy at the boundary means a misbehaving consumer burns the gateway's budget, not the org's; the shared allocation is finite and enforced on all calls, so a request refused before reaching Salesforce never consumes it.

questions.question: A production org returns REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED even though only a small fraction of the daily allocation is used. What explains this?
options: The concurrent and total allocation limits are the same number measured over two different windows of time.
The timeout limit has expired for the org, which silently cancels every subsequent request for the remainder of the day regardless of size.
The concurrent request limit caps long-running inbound requests, so a burst of them can trip it while the daily total stays low.
Only calls that complete faster than twenty seconds count toward any of the platform's limits.
questions.explanation: The concurrent limit caps inbound requests lasting twenty seconds or longer, and it is distinct from the rolling total allocation, so several long-running calls at once can trip it even while the daily total remains well under its cap.

questions.question: A team changes the response shape of a live API but keeps the same version number. Why is this a mistake?
options: A version is a promise, so quietly changing its behavior breaks tenants; a breaking change needs a new major version and a deprecation window.
It is only ever a problem if the change is made in a sandbox rather than in the production org.
It is fine as long as the team notifies every consumer by email after the updated response has already shipped to production and settled for a few days.
New versions should never be created, so keeping the existing version number is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: A version is a contract with its consumers, so quietly altering an existing version's behavior is how worked-yesterday incidents start; a breaking change belongs in a new major version kept alongside the old one through a deprecation window.
